problem: Added hedge "perhaps" not in source ("except it be of the climate and the soil").
replacement: Nothing is more embarrassing in the ordinary course of life than this irritable patriotism of the Americans. A stranger may be quite willing to praise many of the institutions of their country, but he asks permission to criticize some of the peculiarities he observes, and that permission is firmly refused. America is therefore a free country in which, lest anyone be hurt by your remarks, you are not allowed to speak freely of private individuals or of the State, of the citizens or of the authorities, of public or of private undertakings, or in short of anything at all, except the climate and the soil. And even then Americans will be found ready to defend one or the other, as if the inhabitants of the country had designed them.

problem: "national peculiarities" rendered "national character", shifting the sense.
replacement: This truth is shown in the most trivial details of national peculiarities. In France very few pleasures are kept for the higher classes alone. The poor are admitted wherever the rich are received, so they behave properly and respect whatever adds to the enjoyments they share. In England, where wealth monopolizes amusement as well as power, people complain that when the poor happen to sneak into the grounds set aside for the pleasures of the rich, they commit acts of wanton mischief. Is that surprising, when care has been taken that they should have nothing to lose? *b

problem: The causal "for as" in "I am wrong, however, in saying all classes; for as in America..." was dropped, so the reason for the correction is no longer stated.
replacement: But I am wrong to say all classes, for in America the European scale of authority is inverted, and the wealthy are placed in a position like that of the poor in the Old World. It is the wealthy classes that often regard the law with suspicion. I have already observed that the advantage of democracy is not, as has sometimes been claimed, that it protects the interests of the whole community, but simply that it protects those of the majority. In the United States, where the poor rule, the rich always have some reason to fear the abuse of the poor’s power. This natural anxiety of the rich may produce a sullen dissatisfaction, but society is not disturbed by it. For the same reason that leads the rich to withhold their confidence from the legislative authority makes them obey its commands: their wealth, which prevents them from making the law, prevents them from resisting it. Among civilized nations, revolts are rarely stirred up except by people who have nothing to lose by them. And if the laws of a democracy are not always worthy of respect, at least they always obtain it. For those who usually break the laws have no excuse for not complying with enactments that they have made themselves and from which they benefit. Meanwhile the citizens whose interests might be served by breaking the laws are led, by their character and their position, to submit to the decisions of the legislature, whatever they may be. Besides, the people in America obey the law not only because it comes from the popular authority, but because that authority can change it in any point that proves vexatious. A law is obeyed because it is, first, an evil the people have imposed on themselves, and second, an evil of short duration.

d [ The same observation was made at Rome under the first Caesars. Somewhere Montesquieu mentions the excessive despondency of certain Roman citizens who, after the excitement of political life, were suddenly thrown back into the stagnation of private life.]
